This report (2023‑102.2) focuses primarily on the activities of the two cities we reviewed, San José and San Diego, and it concludes that the cities must do more to better evaluate their efforts to reduce homelessness. San José and San Diego identified hundreds of millions of dollars in spending of federal, state, and local funding in recent years to respond to the homelessness crisis. However, neither city could definitively identify all its revenues and expenditures related to its homelessness efforts because neither has an established mechanism, such as a spending plan, to track and report its spending. The absence of such a mechanism limits the transparency and accountability of the cities’ uses of funding to address homelessness. Although both cities provide tens of millions of dollars for homelessness programs and services through agreements with external service providers, such as nonprofits, neither city evaluated the effectiveness of its agreements. San Diego has generally established clear performance measures, such as specifying the number of people the service provider will assist, to enable it to assess whether the providers’ efforts are an effective use of funds. However, San José has not consistently done so. Furthermore, neither city has evaluated the effectiveness of the programs it provides to address the profound health and safety risks associated with unsheltered homelessness. Both cities use interim housing as a way to provide shelter for people experiencing homelessness, but they both need to develop additional permanent housing. Data consistently show that placements into permanent housing results in significantly better outcomes than placements into interim housing. Beginning in November 2017, t he City took initial steps to wards address ing homelessness with the establishment of three bridge shelters in response to a Hepatitis A outbreak that dis proportionately affected those experiencing homelessness . The operation s of the three shelters were initially funded with $6.5 million in SDHC funds on a one -time basis for a partial year . In FY 2024, the program is expected to total around $20 million . Shortly after establishing the bridge shelters , the City established the first of three storage facilit ies and the Homelessness Response Center . In December 2018, the City Council approved the first of a series of one -time multi -year State grants, summarized below. M ost notably , State funds include the Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention Program (HHAP) grant s, which have been used to partially fund the bridge shelters as well as continue the expansion of homelessness services. These grants have supported a wide range of homelessness programs, including storage facilities, outreach, safe parking, prevention and diversion, family reunification, flexible spending, landlord engagement, and ra pid rehousing. Thus, much of the program expansions since the creation of the bridge shelter programs were funded with one -time grant resources , creating a structural deficit in the homelessness budget . For example, in one assessment that San José performed of a $2 million amendment to an agreement for rapid rehousing services, city staff assessed a provider’s performance as “adequate.” However, the city staff’s description in the assessment of the provider’s performance indicated that the provider had failed to meet nearly all activity goals for the year. While the provider did not meet the contract performance targets, the city believes the performance was adequate given difficult circumstances related to moving people from an encampment into housing and agreed that it could have better documented why its assessment of the performance was adequate. We identified similar problems with San Diego’s performance assessments. The housing commission explained that it uses its monthly data collection tools to compare results of a program to the contracted benchmarks and that it bases these contracted benchmarks on its CoC's community standards and other best practice information. When we reviewed a data collection tool for an interim housing and supportive services contract, we saw that the service provider was consistently not meeting the stated benchmark of 26 percent exits to permanent housing. In fact, the percentage of exits to permanent housing was 6 percent during the term of the agreement. Given that the provider was falling significantly short of meeting this benchmark, we would have expected the housing commission to analyze the provider's performance to determine whether the agreement was effective. However, the data collection tool did not include such an analysis from the commission. Although both cities asserted that they monitored or reviewed the performance of their service providers, their staff did not always document overall conclusions about the effectiveness of the service providers’ efforts. synthesis.title: San Diego homelessness spending: incomplete cost accounting, temporary backfills, restroom-service ambiguity, and unresolved contract-effectiveness questions
synthesis.summary: The retrieved records support five concrete leads. First, San Diego’s published FY 2024 and FY 2027 homelessness funding tables explicitly exclude CleanSD encampment-abatement and Police Neighborhood Policing Division costs, matching the State Auditor’s warning that the City could not definitively identify all homelessness revenues and expenditures. Second, the FY 2025 budget used an $8.0 million Affordable Housing Fund contribution to balance existing homelessness programs despite a documented structural deficit, and FY 2027 later adopted visible service reductions. Third, the proposed Kettner/Vine 1,000-bed shelter showed only $1.9 million identified in the FY 2025 adopted budget against an estimated operating cost of up to $30.7 million annually, with no later legislative or payment file retrieved here. Fourth, FY 2027 explicitly cut Downtown public restrooms, but the annual homelessness tables also omit some sanitation and enforcement costs, so the retrieved reports cannot show whether bathroom and waste-response capacity actually fell citywide or shifted elsewhere. Fifth, the State Auditor documented at least one SDHC-monitored contract with 6 percent exits to permanent housing against a 26 percent benchmark without documented effectiveness analysis. The most useful next records are the Item 605 legislative file, Downtown restroom closure and replacement records, the Kettner/Vine lease and operating file, the $8.0 million transfer records, citywide reconciliations that add CleanSD and Police NPD actuals, and SDHC’s contract-specific monitoring and reimbursement files.

findings.title: Annual homelessness funding tables still exclude encampment-abatement and Police NPD costs
findings.interpretation: The FY 2024 and FY 2027 homelessness funding reports explicitly say their tables omit CleanSD encampment abatement, the Police Department’s Neighborhood Policing Division, and other direct or indirect departmental costs. That is consistent with the State Auditor’s conclusion that San Diego lacked a mechanism to definitively identify all homelessness revenues and expenditures. The supported conclusion is narrower than total nontransparency: the retrieved annual homelessness tables are not, by themselves, a complete citywide spending reconciliation.
findings.whyItMatters: Without those omitted costs, the public cannot fairly compare reductions in shelters, safe parking, restrooms, or day-center services against the City’s full homelessness-response footprint.

citations.quote: The table does not capture all homelessness -related expenses such as homeless encampment abatement through CleanSD, the Police Department's Neighborhood Policing Division, or other costs related to direct or indirect department involvement with those experiencing ho melessness.

The table does not capture all homelessness - related expenses such as homeless encampment abatement through CleanSD, the Police Department's Neighborhood Policing Division, or other costs related to direct or indirect department involvement with those expe riencing homelessness.

neither city could definitively identify all its revenues and expenditures related to its homelessness efforts because neither has an established mechanism, such as a spending plan, to track and report its spending.

counterEvidence.quote: this annual report aims to consolidate these actions and funding sources into one document for easier reference.
We note that HSSD staff reports on HSSD -funded homelessness expenditures in a memorandum attached to quarterly budget monitoring reports.

alternativeExplanations: The omission may be an intentional scope choice to show direct service programs rather than every citywide homelessness-related cost.
Separate departmental or quarterly documents may already reconcile some omitted costs, but they were not retrieved in this bounded set.
Police and CleanSD costs may be tracked internally without being integrated into the public annual homelessness report.
findings.nextTest: Obtain FY 2024 through FY 2027 HSSD quarterly expenditure memoranda and any Department of Finance crosswalks that add CleanSD and Police NPD adopted budgets and actuals back into the homelessness reporting framework.

findings.title: The $8.0 million Affordable Housing Fund contribution looks like a bridge, not a solved recurring funding source
findings.interpretation: The retrieved sequence is concrete: the City reported that many homelessness program expansions relied on one-time grants and created "a structural deficit," then reported that FY 2025 used $8.0 million from the Affordable Housing Fund to fill the gap for existing programs, and by FY 2027 the adopted budget included visible closures or reductions. This does not prove the Affordable Housing Fund transfer caused the later cuts, but it supports a lead that the transfer was temporary gap-filling rather than a durable recurring fix.
findings.whyItMatters: The central policy question is whether shifting $8.0 million away from affordable-housing uses bought enough service continuity to justify the tradeoff, or mainly postponed later reductions.

citations.quote: much of the program expansions since the creation of the bridge shelter programs were funded with one -time grant resources , creating a structural deficit in the homelessness budget .

The use of $8.0 million from the Affordable Housing Fund to fill the funding gap for existing homelessness programs along with less available one - time HHAP funding anticipated in future year s signal s the potential for serious challenges in identifying sufficient ongoing revenue to support homelessness expenditures
the FY 2025 homelessness budget was balanced with a $8.0 million contribution from the Afford able Housing Fund, which otherwise would have gone towards affordable housing and other programs

These reductions included closure of the City -funded Lighthouse Shelter (although the site will continue to operate as a different program without City funds) , two safe parking sites, and Downtown public restrooms, as well as the reduction of the 16 th and Newton Shelter and the Neil Good Day Center

counterEvidence.quote: prevention and diversion funding is budgeted to increase by $4. 3 million relative to the prior year, largely due to local philanthropic grants secured by SDHC . City funding for substance use disorder treatment shelters is also expected to increase on net due to additional planned opioid treatment beds funded by Opioid Settlement Funds.

alternativeExplanations: The City may have intentionally shifted its mix from some shelter and restroom operations toward prevention, diversion, or treatment.
Some reduced programs may have continued with philanthropic, County, or provider funding outside the City budget.
The later reductions may reflect multiple pressures at once, including reduced HHAP availability and a broader General Fund reduction target, not just the Affordable Housing Fund transfer.
findings.nextTest: Retrieve the transfer authorizations, fund and account coding, and decision memos for the $8.0 million contribution, then compare FY 2025 through FY 2027 actual expenditures, occupancy, exits to permanent housing, and closure or wind-down costs for the programs it preserved against any affordable-housing activities deferred or reduced.

findings.title: The Kettner/Vine 1,000-bed proposal shows a visible budget-to-obligation gap
findings.interpretation: The FY 2025 report says the adopted budget included $1.9 million for additional shelter beds tied to a proposed 1,000-bed permanent emergency shelter site, but also says the lease was still pending and that operations could cost up to $30.7 million annually and could not be supported within existing City resources without major tradeoffs. In this bounded retrieval, no later legislative file, executed lease, or payment record explains whether the concept was approved, revised, relocated, or abandoned. The supported discrepancy is between a limited identified FY 2025 amount and a much larger contingent recurring obligation.
findings.whyItMatters: Large shelter proposals can look funded in budget documents even when only a small initial amount is identified and the full operating plan remains unresolved.

citations.quote: The FY 202 5 Adopted Budget includes $ 1.9 million for additional shelter beds, currently proposed for a 1,000 - bed permanent emergency shelter site – the lease for the site located at Kettner Blvd and Vine St was fi rst presented to City Council on July 22, 2024.

Although the lease is still pending, if approved, the operation of the shelter program is estimated to cost up to $30.7 million annually , which cannot be supported within existing City resources without significant tradeoffs with other City services .
various reductions were contemplated by HSSD, the Mayor’s Office, SDHC, and the Council to meet a 7% reduction target in the City’s General Fund

alternativeExplanations: The lease may have been rejected or materially revised before execution, eliminating the longer-term cost issue.
The $30.7 million figure may have been a high-end scenario that later changed with a different operator, scope, or outside funding package.
The project may have moved to another site or another budget vehicle not retrieved here.
findings.nextTest: Retrieve the July 22, 2024 legislative file, any executed lease or termination records, operator procurement documents, operating pro formas, encumbrances, and payment records tied to Kettner/Vine or any successor site.

findings.title: FY 2027 cut Downtown public restrooms, but the public reports do not show whether sanitation services shifted elsewhere
findings.interpretation: The FY 2027 report explicitly lists "Closure of public restrooms ($750,000)" and elsewhere describes reductions that included "Downtown public restrooms." The same report says its tables do not capture CleanSD encampment abatement and other indirect departmental costs. The supported conclusion is limited but important: the homelessness report confirms a line-item reduction in restroom funding, yet the retrieved annual reports cannot show whether public bathroom and waste-response capacity actually fell citywide or was transferred to another department or grant.
findings.whyItMatters: Bathroom access and waste management are direct health and encampment-response issues. If a restroom cut was offset elsewhere, the public should see that; if not, the cut may have broader sanitation consequences than the homelessness tables reveal.

citations.quote: Closure of public restrooms ($750,000) and Day Center ($711,000); State grant spend-down ($1.4M); PEER College course funding removed ($94,000)

These reductions included closure of the City -funded Lighthouse Shelter (although the site will continue to operate as a different program without City funds) , two safe parking sites, and Downtown public restrooms, as well as the reduction of the 16 th and Newton Shelter and the Neil Good Day Center

The table does not capture all homelessness - related expenses such as homeless encampment abatement through CleanSD, the Police Department's Neighborhood Policing Division, or other costs related to direct or indirect department involvement with those expe riencing homelessness.

counterEvidence.quote: this annual report aims to consolidate these actions and funding sources into one document for easier reference.

alternativeExplanations: Restroom access may have been replaced by portable facilities or nearby public facilities funded outside the homelessness budget.
CleanSD or another department may have absorbed part of the sanitation response without labeling it as homelessness spending.
The closure may have reflected a site move, low utilization, or a provider change rather than a simple citywide service loss.
findings.nextTest: Obtain the Downtown restroom closure plan, any replacement sanitation or portable-restroom contracts, location and hours tables, CleanSD work orders and actuals, and any cross-department briefing that explains how restroom and waste services changed after the FY 2027 cut.

findings.title: SDHC’s described monitoring process is hard to reconcile with the auditor’s 26%-benchmark and 6%-actual contract example
findings.interpretation: The State Auditor found an interim-housing and supportive-services contract in which the provider achieved 6 percent exits to permanent housing against a 26 percent benchmark, and auditors did not find documented analysis by the Housing Commission on whether the agreement was effective. Elsewhere in the same record, SDHC describes reimbursement review, quarterly check-ins, and technical-assistance processes. That combination suggests a concrete risk that SDHC tracked data and held monitoring meetings without preserving a formal decision trail showing how poor outcomes affected renewals, amendments, or reimbursements. The excerpt does not identify the provider, so this remains a contract-identification lead rather than a systemwide conclusion.
findings.whyItMatters: This is the clearest contract-specific cost-effectiveness lead in the record. If underperforming contracts kept receiving payments or extensions without documented analysis, decisionmakers could not easily tell whether funding was buying permanent exits or mainly preserving bed inventory.

citations.quote: the service provider was consistently not meeting the stated benchmark of 26 percent exits to permanent housing. In fact, the percentage of exits to permanent housing was 6 percent during the term of the agreement.

we would have expected the housing commission to analyze the provider's performance to determine whether the agreement was effective. However, the data collection tool did not include such an analysis from the commission.

Quarterly Check-In Meetings and Technical Assistance Plans: SDHC’s Homelessness Innovations Division’s Policies and Procedures describe the method for facilitating the quarterly meetings and detail the items to be included on the agenda such as reviewing budget utilization, program outcomes, and other items identified as requiring more technical assistance.

counterEvidence.quote: San Diego has generally established clear performance measures, such as specifying the number of people the service provider will assist, to enable it to assess whether the providers’ efforts are an effective use of funds.

alternativeExplanations: The provider may have served a higher-acuity or unusually difficult population, making the benchmark unrealistic.
SDHC may have performed an effectiveness analysis informally but failed to preserve it in the tool reviewed by auditors.
The example may have been an outlier rather than representative of SDHC’s broader contract portfolio.
findings.nextTest: Identify the specific contract and provider in the audit example, then review the contract file, amendments, reimbursements, quarterly monitoring records, technical-assistance plans, and any renewal or non-renewal recommendation after the 6 percent result.

questions.question: Do the Item 605 staff report and attachments show that the $3,666,572 amendment is restricted to riverbed-specific outreach, medical, or housing services rather than general shelter, restroom, or day-center operations?
questions.why: The FY 2027 report documents local cuts, while the September 28, 2026 agenda shows a near-contemporaneous new appropriation and term extension. Scope restrictions would help distinguish net new services from a substitution story.

questions.question: After the FY 2027 closure of Downtown public restrooms, what replacement sanitation access, if any, was funded through other departments or grants, and at which locations?
questions.why: The report explicitly shows a restroom closure, but the same annual tables exclude CleanSD and other indirect departmental costs. Without the replacement record, the public cannot tell whether access actually fell or merely moved off the homelessness report.

questions.question: After the FY 2027 budget reductions, which specific programs actually continued under non-City funding or reduced-capacity arrangements, especially Lighthouse Shelter and the Neil Good Day Center, and who funded and administered the successor operations?
questions.why: The FY 2027 report makes continuity claims for both sites. The interpretation weakens if no executed successor agreement or funding stream exists.

questions.question: What became of the proposed 1,000-bed permanent emergency shelter at Kettner Blvd and Vine St after FY 2025 budgeted $1.9 million for added beds but warned that operations could cost up to $30.7 million annually?
questions.why: This is one of the clearest appropriation-to-obligation gaps in the record. The lead would weaken if later Council action shows the lease was denied, materially changed, relocated, or largely funded outside the General Fund.

questions.question: Is there any later citywide reconciliation that adds omitted homelessness-related costs from CleanSD encampment abatement, the Police Department's Neighborhood Policing Division, and other indirect departmental work back into the published homelessness budget?
questions.why: This remains the biggest completeness gap in any budget-to-spending trace. The annual reports explicitly exclude those costs, while the State Auditor said San Diego lacked a mechanism to definitively identify all homelessness revenues and expenditures.

questions.question: Can we identify the specific San Diego interim-housing or supportive-services contract in the State Auditor example with a 26 percent permanent-housing benchmark and only 6 percent actual exits, then test whether it later received renewals, amendments, or continued reimbursements?
questions.why: This would turn a general audit criticism into a contract-specific accountability trail. The concern would weaken if the agreement ended, reimbursements stopped, or later monitoring documented improved performance before new funding.

questions.question: What actual FY 2025 and FY 2026 expenditures, occupancy or utilization, exits to permanent housing, and closure or wind-down costs were recorded for the programs preserved by the $8.0 million Affordable Housing Fund contribution, and which affordable-housing uses were delayed or displaced to free that money?
questions.why: This directly tests whether the Affordable Housing Fund transfer bought measurable continuity or mainly postponed cuts while reducing housing investment elsewhere.

questions.question: For the two Homekey permanent supportive housing projects that drove the FY 2025 budget spike, what were the acquisition amounts, local match sources, units delivered, occupancy dates, and housing-retention outcomes by FY 2027?
questions.why: FY 2025's large increase was reported as mostly one-time Homekey money, and FY 2027 shows those one-time funds rolling off after acquisition. Project-level outputs are needed so capital spikes are not mistaken for recurring service expansion.
